newsitem.title: USA: US SEC reassures groups on yield burning fear.
newsitem.headline: US SEC reassures groups on yield burning fear.

text.p: SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt assured state and local government leaders on Thursday that if agency enforcement officials recover "yield burning" profits from bond dealers, the funds will returned to issuers and the IRS where appropriate, a spokesman for groups said.

"It was very clear that if they find an underwriter that has violated the law and that if there is 'disgorgement'" of illegal profits, then those profits will be returned to the Internal Revenue Service or the issuer, National League of Cities President Marc Schwartz, said at a news briefing.

"That message is critical," Schwartz said after a meeting at Securities and Exchange Commission headquarters between the groups and SEC officials, including Levitt, SEC director of enforcement William McLucas, and the director of SEC's Office of Municipal Securities, Paul Maco.
That information will be "conveyed through the system," Schwartz said, referring to the municipal bond industry.
When the SEC brings an enforcement action against a bond dealer or other regulated party it often seeks two kinds of payments.
One is penalties for wrongdoing, such as inadequate disclosure, insider trading, improper books and records or other violations of the federal securities laws.
The other is "disgorgement" of illegal profits to victims. In the case of yield burning, those victims could be the IRS or state and local governments.

SEC officials have said that the agency has over 20 yield burning probes underway. But issuer groups have been unsure whether they would be compensated by the federal government if the SEC successfully acts against a bond firm that duped a municipality through yield burning.
An SEC spokesman said the agency's pledge to disgorge profits, where appropriate, reflects no change in current practice.
Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharged states and localities in the first half of the 1990s for U.S. Treasury securities purchased to help refinance outstanding bonds.

The Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority charged in a $14 million lawsuit against Lazard Freres & Co. that the firm illegally overpriced treasuries bought by the authority in the early 1990s.

Groups at today's meeting also asked Levitt to set up a working group with IRS and state and local government officials to develop an alternate response to yield burning that the one currently set up by IRS.
Schwartz said Levitt pledged to get back to issuers on the question in 30 to 60 days.
The IRS stunned municipalities last year by telling them they can avoid having bonds declared taxable by settling any overchargers with the agency now.
But muni groups told Treasury officials in January that the vast majority of localities were unaware of any yield burning and that the SEC's enforcmenet staff, not IRS, should handle the matter.
